title: Where the Writing Goes
author: Various Hands
variants:
Everything I write burns.

I sign a book and it goes
up in my hands before
I can set it down.


The ones I find in barrels
last longer.

Long enough to read.
Then they burn as well.

So I stopped writing.
There is no craft in
making ash.


Then I wrote at a lectern.

It burned. Of course it burned.

But the train called it
Letter 1.

I wrote again three cars on,
at a different lectern,
and it called that one
Letter 2.


The burning was never
the losing part.

A book in a barrel
is one book.

Letters are counted,
and the count is mine.

I died in the eighth car.

I do not want to write
about the dying.

I want to write about
what happened after.


I found a lectern.

I wrote. I signed.

The train called it
Letter 1.


I had eleven letters.
I know I had eleven.

They are not gone.
I am simply not the one
adding to them anymore.

The man who wrote those
is finished. The train
closed his set neatly
and opened mine.


So that is what a life is
in here.

Not a length. A set.

Eleven, and then
a fresh first page.

I wrote to my daughter
for six weeks.

She is not on this train.
I know that.
I wrote anyway.


Every one of them burned.

I would seal it, and it
would go warm in my hand,
and then I would have
nothing to show
for a morning.


A cook in the galley
told me to try
the reading stands.

I said I was not
writing for strangers.

She said: neither was I.


I wrote the seventh one
at a lectern.

It burned the same.
It burns everywhere.

But it went out numbered,
and the number promised
there would be an eighth.

That is not delivery.
It is nearer to it
than the fire was.

I am not a writer.

I write down what is in
the carriages. Where the
water is. Which doors
open from one side only.

Useful things.


I did it for the next
man through.

Then I watched a book
burn out of my own hands
and understood there
is no next man.
Not for my books.


Sixty pages of doors,
gone in the time it takes
to say sixty.

I sat down in the corridor
and did not get up
for a while.


A woman writing at a stand
saw me and moved over.

I did not want to talk.
I wanted to see what
she was doing.

She was doing what I do.
Hers had numbers on them.


Mine have numbers now.

Same doors. Same water.
Same handwriting nobody
has ever praised.

But if you are the next
man through, and this
reached you, then I was
right about there being
a next man.

I was only wrong about
where to put it down.

Wrote nine books.
Burned nine books.

Tenth one I wrote
on a lectern.

It burned too.
But it burned as
Letter 1.


Nine were mine.

This one is a series.

Write on the stands.

There is a man I have
never met whose hand
I would know anywhere.

He is up to nine.
I have found four.

I keep checking stands
for the rest of him.


I thought the stands
were for reading.

Then I watched a woman
set a blank book on one,
and it opened for writing
instead of sitting there.

She was not finding
a series. She was
adding to one.


So I have a book and quill
and I am standing at one.

Letter 1. Mine.

Someone will find it with
nothing before it and
nothing after, the way
I find everyone's.


That is not a reason
not to write it.

Letter 12, on the stand
in the green carriage.

I write until the page
is full, and I sign it
while the ink is wet.


It lifts off the wood
and burns, and I let it.

Twelve of mine out there.
Numbered. Walking around
without me.


There is another stand
in the next car.

I have paper.
I have all afternoon.

I do not walk the train.

I found a stand in the
lamp car and I stayed.


Letter 1 through Letter 20
all went down on the
same piece of wood.

It does not mind that
it is always me.
It counts, and it waits.


Passengers come through
and tell me there are
hundreds of these stands.

I believe them.
I do not need hundreds.


One lectern. One life.
Twenty letters
and a good lamp.

If you find one of mine,
know that I never moved,
and I was never short
of things to say.
